Oregon’s pioneering effort to decriminalize possession of small amounts of hard drugs is set to expire on Sunday. A new statute, HB4002, will once again classify such possession as a crime, but it gives individuals stopped with substances like fentanyl, heroin or meth a choice: face a criminal charge or enter a treatment pathway that includes a behavioral‑health program and a deflection initiative designed to avoid fines.  
***  
Under the law, personal‑use possession becomes a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail. The measure aims to give police more authority to address drug use in public spaces and imposes steeper penalties for selling drugs near parks. While it urges counties to develop treatment alternatives that divert people from the criminal justice system toward addiction and mental‑health services, it does not require them to do so.  
***  
Supporters argue that this flexibility lets each county tailor programs to its own resources and needs. Critics warn that the approach could produce a confusing and uneven patchwork of rules across the state. Portland police chief Bob Day explained that to qualify for deflection a person must have no other charges, no outstanding warrants, no violent behavior and be medically stable.  
***  
When an individual meets those criteria, officers contact the county’s deflection dispatch line to share basic information, verify eligibility and summon a mobile behavioral‑health outreach team. The team has thirty minutes to arrive; if they cannot be on scene within that time, the person is taken to jail. Chief Day said officers cannot afford to wait longer.  

P.P.S. In considering how policies affect people of every age across the country, one might reflect on daily habits such as what we eat, how we enjoy shopping, and even the way we speak, noting the role of our tongue in communication.
